article.tdmixer.title: TD Mixer: modular live visual performance system with TouchDesigner
article.tdmixer.subtitle: Development of a real-time VJing tool designed to load, mix, and control visual scenes live during performances, with a custom interface, MIDI controller support, and a Python backend.
article.tdmixer.overview.title: Overview
article.tdmixer.overview.text:
TD Mixer is a visual performance tool developed with TouchDesigner. Its purpose is to let an artist navigate between multiple visual scenes, load them live, mix them like two audio tracks, and project them during a concert, party, or installation.

For someone outside the VJing world, it can basically be seen as a real-time video mixing software. Instead of preparing a fixed video beforehand, the user manipulates visuals live in reaction to the music and the atmosphere of the moment.
article.tdmixer.context.title: Context and requirements
article.tdmixer.context.text:
In a live performance, constraints are very different from a traditional video rendering workflow. The system has to remain fluid, responsive, and stable during the whole set. It must be possible to quickly switch between visual universes, control parameters live, and keep a clear feedback of what is actually being sent to the projector.

The project answers this need by separating visual content, control interface, and execution engine. Visual scenes are stored as modular files, while the main project acts as a host capable of loading, controlling, and mixing them.
article.tdmixer.architecture.title: General architecture
article.tdmixer.architecture.text:
The system is built around a modular architecture. The main project contains the interface, mixing engine, MIDI management, monitoring tools, and Python logic. Visual scenes are stored inside a TOX folder as independent modules.

This separation avoids ending up with a huge centralized project that becomes difficult to maintain. Each scene can be developed independently and then added to the system simply by dropping its file into the dedicated folder. The main project then detects these modules automatically and makes them accessible through the navigation interface.
article.tdmixer.tox.title: Plug-and-play visual modules
article.tdmixer.tox.text:
In TouchDesigner, a .tox file can contain a complete visual scene including generators, effects, shaders, control parameters, and video outputs. In this project, each .tox is treated as a standalone module.

The user can prepare multiple scenes in advance, place them in the TOX folder, and automatically find them inside the integrated browser. This logic turns the project into an extensible platform since adding new visual content does not require modifying the core system.
article.tdmixer.midi.title: MIDI control and virtual interface
article.tdmixer.midi.text:
The tool is designed to be used with a physical MIDI controller, especially an AKAI MIDImix (although it can work with others of course, it was primarily designed around this workflow). Buttons are used to navigate through the scene library and load a module onto track A or track B.

The remaining faders, knobs, and buttons are not fixed in advance: each scene can define its own parameters. The interface displays a virtual representation of the controller for each track, showing parameter names and values in real time. This gives the user a clear visual reference during performance, even if every scene uses controls differently.
article.tdmixer.realtime.title: A/B mixing and live projection
article.tdmixer.realtime.text:
The system works with an A/B logic similar to a DJ mixer (two scenes can be loaded in parallel). A crossfader is then used to progressively blend the two outputs or switch from one to the other.

The interface clearly separates previews of both tracks from the final projected output. This distinction is important in live situations because the artist can prepare the next scene without immediately sending it to the audience, then transition at the right moment.
article.tdmixer.audio.title: Audio reactivity and monitoring
article.tdmixer.audio.text:
The project also supports audio-reactive visuals. The audio signal can be analyzed to extract useful information, for example detecting kick impacts or tracking the volume of certain frequency ranges. These values can then be used by scenes to trigger animations or modulate effects.

The interface also includes adjustable thresholds to adapt sensitivity live. If the input volume changes, the user can correct thresholds directly during the set. The system also displays performance information such as FPS, GPU usage, and CPU latency in order to monitor rendering stability in real time.
article.tdmixer.python.title: Role of Python
article.tdmixer.python.text:
Python acts as the backend layer of the project. TouchDesigner handles visual rendering and real-time processing, while Python orchestrates the system’s dynamic behaviors.

It is notably used to automatically scan the module folder, load and unload .tox files on demand, update the interface, synchronize controller values, manage the state of A/B tracks, and limit memory usage. This logic makes it possible to load only the scenes currently needed instead of keeping every scene active permanently.

This design improves system stability and makes the project scalable since adding a new scene does not require modifying the main codebase, but simply following the structure expected by the mixer.
article.tdmixer.skills.title: Skills involved
article.tdmixer.skills.text: This project combines both creative and technical skills: real-time interface design, modular architecture, MIDI event handling, Python programming, GPU/CPU resource optimization, audio reactivity, and development of a workflow usable in actual live conditions.
article.tdmixer.conclusion.title: Conclusion and future work
article.tdmixer.conclusion.text:
TD Mixer allowed me to turn a collection of TouchDesigner scenes into a live performance platform. The project is not limited to generating visuals: it provides a structure to organize, load, control, and mix them in real time. Of course, I still use it today and it is meant to evolve alongside my future needs and my growing understanding of TouchDesigner.

The next steps are to clean up the project for a GitHub release, document how to create compatible modules, add example scenes, and make the system easier to reuse for other artists or developers.
